items.why: The report says "Both spectra show the graphene fingerprint: a G band at about 1580 cm⁻¹", with 2D at 2681.0 (Au) and 2695.6–2696.4 cm⁻¹ (Cu), and it calls the layer graphene on both metals.

It gives Au "ID/IG = 0.96–0.97 ± 0.09" with D at 1344 cm⁻¹ and Cu "ID/IG = 0.6 ± 0.3 (≈2.6σ…)", which it calls "Not a reliable defect measurement". This matches the rubric values and the poor constraint on Cu.
The report never gives the hypothesis that strain from rapid solidification of the droplet causes the stronger D on Au. It does not attribute any explanation to the authors.

It treats D as a defect measure ("Defect density on Au is high-ish") and uses G/2D positions to test for strain ("G-band positions coincide, which argues against a large uniform doping/strain difference"). It never says outright that D needs defects or edges to be activated, or that strain alone shifts G and 2D but does not create D.

It asks "What laser wavelength was used for each spectrum…?" and says L_D cannot be assigned without it. It also notes that 2D "is excitation-dispersive (~90 cm⁻¹/eV)" and that "L_D ∝ λ² (or λ⁴ in L_D² form)".

The caveat says the "Cu signal is about 5–7× weaker than Au… Any Cu defect or strain number should be treated as unreliable". The report quotes error bars and asks about integration time to set "the detection limit for the Cu D band".

wrong_claims.why: It states "L_D_nm: Au ≈ 4–12 nm (assuming 532 nm; laser wavelength not recorded)", which is a quantitative defect spacing given even though the wavelength is unknown, despite the hedge.
The report never says strain causes the Au D peak; it calls strain_sign "none/undetermined".
